introduction: Back in the expedition of 401 BCE, Cyrus’s army halts at Tarsus. The soldiers suspect a war against the Great King and say that this is not the service for which they were hired. Their concern about risk and consent is legitimate.

Course adaptation of Xenophon, Anabasis 1.3.1–21. The refusal, violence against Clearchus, speeches, private message to Cyrus, negotiation, Abrocomas explanation, and increased pay follow the source. The short Greek speeches are newly written summaries, not quotations. The Great King remains a suspicion here: the public announcement comes at Thapsacus in Lesson 19.

The narrative uses present tense. Supplementary noun tables include ships, cattle, and cities without placing every example in this historical scene. Blue glosses support names, contracted forms, and less familiar constructions.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Κῦρος καὶ οἱ στρατιῶται ἐν Ταρσοῖς μένουσιν. ἡ πόλις ἐν Κιλικίᾳ ἐστίν. οἱ δὲ στρατιῶται οὐκ ἐθέλουσι πορεύεσθαι· ὑποπτεύουσι γὰρ πόλεμον πρὸς τὸν μέγαν βασιλέα.
Τῶν στρατιωτῶν οἱ μὲν λέγουσιν· «οὐ πρὸς τὸν βασιλέα στρατευόμεθα· οὐκ ἐπὶ τοῦτο μισθούμεθα.» ὁ Κλέαρχος πρῶτον βίᾳ ἄγει τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ στρατιώτας. οἱ δὲ λίθους βάλλουσιν εἰς αὐτὸν καὶ τὰ ὑποζύγια.
Ἡ βία οὐκ ὠφελεῖ. ὁ Κλέαρχος τῶν ἑαυτοῦ στρατιωτῶν ἐκκλησίαν ποιεῖ καὶ δακρύει. οἱ παρόντες σιωπῶσιν. ὁ δὲ λέγει· «ὑμεῖς ἐμοὶ φίλοι καὶ σύμμαχοί ἐστε· ἐγὼ μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν μένω.»

Οἱ ἀκούοντες ἐπαινοῦσι τὸν Κλέαρχον. πολλοὶ τῶν ἄλλων στρατιωτῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔρχονται. ὁ δὲ Κῦρος αὐτὸν καλεῖ· ὁ Κλέαρχος οὐκ ἔρχεται, ἀλλὰ λάθρᾳ ἄγγελον πέμπει. τῷ Κύρῳ ἀγγέλλει· «θάρρει· τὰ πράγματα καλῶς ἔχει.»

reading.translation:
Cyrus and the soldiers remain at Tarsus. The city is in Cilicia. The soldiers are unwilling to march; for they suspect a war against the Great King.

Some of the soldiers say, “We are not serving against the King; we are not hired for this.” Clearchus first leads his own soldiers by force. They throw stones at him and the pack animals.

Force does not help. Clearchus holds an assembly of his own soldiers and weeps. Those present are silent. He says, “You are my friends and allies; I remain with you.”

The listeners praise Clearchus. Many of the other soldiers come to him. Cyrus summons him; Clearchus does not come but secretly sends a messenger. He reports to Cyrus, “Take heart; matters are going well.”

In the assembly some seek the road home, while others speak about boats and guides. It is difficult to depart without Cyrus’s agreement. Supplies are in Cyrus’s market.

The soldiers send representatives to Cyrus. The representatives ask, “What do you want?” He says, “Abrocomas is my enemy; I want to march against him.” The representatives report the answer to the soldiers.

The soldiers still suspect the war against the King, but nevertheless decide to follow. They ask for greater pay, and Cyrus promises pay half as large again. Yet he does not openly state that he is leading them against the King.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — A request, a suspicion, and an assembly

blocks.title: A request, a suspicion, and an assembly
body: ἐρωτάω asks a question; αἰτέω asks for something. The representatives ἐρωτῶσι τί βούλει, while the soldiers αἰτοῦσι μισθόν. Asking about the plan and asking for pay are related negotiations, but different verb meanings.

ὑποπτεύω means suspect, not know with certainty. Cyrus’s public explanation mentions Abrocomas. The soldiers’ suspicion survives their decision to proceed. Keep the difference between the narrator’s knowledge and the participants’ publicly available information.

ἐκκλησία means an assembly; here it is a soldiers’ gathering rather than Athens’s civic Assembly. οἱ μὲν and οἱ δὲ can divide participants into groups. τὰ ἐπιτήδεια uses an adjective as a noun for the necessities that make remaining or leaving possible.

sections.title: 1. Third-Declension Nouns with -ντ- Stems
body: The participles of Lesson 17 introduced -οντ-. Nouns can also have a ντ stem: γέρων, γέροντος, “old man,” and γίγας, γίγαντος, “giant.” The genitive reveals the stem; the nominative alone may hide part of it.

γέρων has a lengthened nominative and loses final τ. In γίγας the ντ disappears before nominative σ and the α lengthens. Dative plural similarly loses ντ before σ: γέρουσι(ν), γίγασι(ν). Do not insert ντ into those surface forms.

The other cases preserve the stem: γέροντα, γέροντι, γίγαντα, γίγαντι. These are supplementary travel and story examples, not claims that a giant or an old man took a role in the Tarsus negotiations. Learn case by article and ending together.

examples.english: The old man speaks to the old men (supplementary example).
I see the giant (supplementary story example).

checks.answer: γέροντος. Removing -ος from γέροντος gives γεροντ-.

sections.title: 2. πόλις and ἄστυ
body: Vowel-stem nouns do not follow a single unchanging stem spelling. πόλις has genitive πόλεως and dative πόλει. The plural is πόλεις, πόλεων, πόλεσι(ν), πόλεις. The feminine article makes the case clear even when nominative and accusative plural coincide.

ἄστυ is neuter: nominative and accusative singular are both ἄστυ, while genitive is ἄστεως and dative ἄστει. Plural nominative/accusative is ἄστη, genitive ἄστεων, dative ἄστεσι(ν). The neuter article is τὸ or τά in those direct cases.

πόλις often refers to the civic community as well as its city; ἄστυ emphasizes the urban settlement. Since English “city” can translate both in some contexts, vocabulary questions give the exact dictionary sense and avoid using one as a misleading synonym distractor for the other.

examples.english: We remain in the town (supplementary example).

checks.answer: πόλεως. The genitive singular is πόλεως.

checks.prompt: Which is dative singular of πόλις?

sections.title: 3. βασιλεύς, ναῦς, and βοῦς
body: βασιλεύς is masculine and changes across cases: βασιλέως, βασιλεῖ, βασιλέα. Its plural is βασιλεῖς, βασιλέων, βασιλεῦσι(ν), βασιλέας. The reading’s πρὸς τὸν μέγαν βασιλέα uses the accusative because πρός marks the opposed destination.

ναῦς is feminine and irregular. Learn νεώς, νηί, ναῦν in the singular; νῆες, νεῶν, ναυσί(ν), ναῦς in the plural. The accusative plural ναῦς looks like nominative singular, so article and context matter. Boats are proposed in the source negotiations; the paradigms below are supplementary.

βοῦς, usually masculine for an ox here, has βοός, βοΐ, βοῦν; plural βόες, βοῶν, βουσί(ν), βοῦς. The noun can also be feminine for a cow, with the appropriate article. Its inclusion supplies the assigned irregular paradigm without inventing cattle in the source episode.

sections.title: 4. Possession, Relationship, and a Part of a Group
body: A possessive genitive links something to an owner: τὰ τοῦ Κύρου χρήματα, “Cyrus’s money.” A genitive can also identify a relationship or association: οἱ τοῦ Κύρου στρατιῶται, “Cyrus’s soldiers.” The latter does not mean that soldiers are objects he owns.

A partitive genitive names the whole group from which a subset is taken: πολλοὶ τῶν στρατιωτῶν, “many of the soldiers”; τῶν στρατιωτῶν οἱ μέν, “some of the soldiers.” The word expressing the part and the genitive whole work together.

Other genitives come from the governing expression: ἄνευ τῆς Κύρου γνώμης, “without Cyrus’s agreement”; περὶ πλοίων, “about boats.” These differ from the time-within-which genitive of Lesson 16, such as τριῶν ἡμερῶν, “within three days.” Case does not have a single English translation.

sections.title: 5. The Article Identifies and Makes Nouns
body: The article identifies a known person or group: ὁ Κῦρος, “Cyrus”; οἱ στρατιῶται, “the soldiers.” Greek often uses an article with a personal name where English does not. The article’s case helps readers track roles across irregular noun forms.

With an adjective or participle and no noun, the article creates a substantival expression: τὰ ἐπιτήδεια, “the supplies”; οἱ παρόντες, “those present.” An adverbial phrase can also be gathered under the article: οἱ ἐν τῇ πόλει, “those in the city.”

Attributive position keeps the description inside the noun phrase: οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι στρατιῶται or οἱ στρατιῶται οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι, “the brave soldiers.” Predicate position, οἱ στρατιῶται ἀνδρεῖοί εἰσιν, asserts “the soldiers are brave.” Revisit participles similarly: οἱ ἀκούοντες names listeners; ἀκούοντες ἐπαινοῦσι adds their accompanying action.

sections.title: A changed risk and the right to question it
body: At Anabasis 1.3.1 the soldiers refuse to march further because they suspect a campaign against the King and say that this was not what they were hired to do. Their objection concerns the scope of the service and its danger. The source gives grounds for interpreting their refusal as a claim about agreement rather than automatic cowardice.

Clearchus tries force and faces stones aimed at him and his pack animals. The violence is serious, and Xenophon says he nearly dies. Acknowledging the soldiers’ legitimate concern does not require approving every method they use. The episode asks how a commander secures cooperation when the original understanding has become doubtful.

sections.title: Public loyalty and private persuasion
body: Clearchus weeps before an assembly and declares solidarity with his men. Soldiers from other contingents join him. Yet he privately reassures Cyrus and arranges for Cyrus to keep summoning him while he publicly refuses. Xenophon presents conduct that can be read as both concern for his troops and calculated management of the crisis.

The army’s assembly is a place for speeches and collective deliberation, but it is not simply the Athenian democratic Assembly transported into Asia. Clearchus encourages some speakers, and the soldiers depend on Cyrus’s camp for supplies. The reading preserves the tension between speaking openly and shaping what choices seem possible.

sections.title: Leaving also requires resources
body: Speakers discuss vessels, a guide, food, safe routes, and the danger of trusting Cyrus after opposing him. The source also notes harm already done to Cilicians: one speaker fears that people whose property the soldiers have taken could block their departure. The difficulty of going home is logistical and political, not just a lack of resolve.

The negotiated explanation names Abrocomas on the Euphrates. Cyrus promises monthly pay of one and a half darics instead of one, and the troops continue while still suspecting the King as the target. Anabasis 1.3.21 explicitly says that no public announcement of that target occurs here. Additional pay settles the immediate movement without removing the information problem.

questions.prompt: Why is the refusal more than simple disobedience?
questions.answer: The soldiers question a danger and objective they say were outside the service for which they were hired.

questions.prompt: What changes after force fails?
questions.answer: Clearchus turns to speeches, private communication, and negotiation.

questions.prompt: Why is his conduct ambiguous?
questions.answer: He publicly aligns with the soldiers while privately assuring Cyrus that the situation can be managed.

questions.prompt: Why is leaving difficult?
questions.answer: Routes, guides, vessels, supplies, Cyrus’s power, and hostile people create risks.

questions.prompt: What change in pay is promised?
questions.answer: Monthly pay rises from one daric to one and a half darics.

questions.prompt: Is war against the King publicly announced at Tarsus?
questions.answer: No. Suspicion remains; explicit announcement comes later at Thapsacus.

questions.prompt: Which leadership decision in this lesson needs reasons beyond personal bravery?
questions.answer: Securing cooperation requires addressing the agreed service and information, not merely demanding obedience.

questions.answer: Distinguish the author’s reported events and speeches from the course’s simplified wording, supplied examples, and ethical inferences.
